title: Putin Will Not Yield
gist: Michael Kimmage and Maria Lipman argue that although the Ukraine war is inflicting real damage on Russia (deep strikes, fuel shortages, low growth, high inflation), economic pain and pressure will not break Putin's resolve. Only the opening of the paywalled essay is available.

insights.claim: Ukraine's deep strikes into Russian territory have increased civilian deaths, disrupted online commerce and caused gasoline shortages inside Russia.
insights.speaker: Michael Kimmage
insights.so_what: Strikes on Russian energy infrastructure tighten domestic fuel supply and can affect refined-product exports; watch Russian fuel export bans.
insights.locator: The war in Ukraine is causing undeniable harm

insights.claim: Burdened by the war, the Russian economy is delivering low growth and high inflation.
insights.speaker: Michael Kimmage
insights.so_what: Stagflation in Russia raises fiscal strain but, per the authors, does not translate into political pressure to end the war.

insights.claim: Prominent Russian banker Andrey Klepach said in May that Russia is falling behind in global technological and economic competition, in some respects even to Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Michael Kimmage
insights.so_what: Elite admissions of economic decline are a signal worth tracking, but not by themselves a sign of policy change.
insights.quote: We are losing the [global] technological and economic competition.
insights.locator: In May, the prominent Russian banker

themes.theme: Pain will not force Putin's hand

insights.claim: Economic pressure and military pain are not expected to sap Russia's resolve or make Putin yield in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Michael Kimmage
insights.so_what: Do not position for an imminent ceasefire driven by sanctions or economic strain; peace-deal trades (e.g., Ukraine reconstruction, Russia reopening) look premature.
insights.quote: Pressure and Pain Won’t Sap Russia’s Resolve in Ukraine
